<!--
Template for kind: "essay" chapters.

A chapter argues or reflects on one idea. It is not a how-to checklist
and it is not a story. Headings are optional; flowing prose is the default.

Universal rules (CLAUDE.md):
- 700-1000 words, Devanagari prose with Roman loanwords (no टॅन्ट्रम).
- Marathi-context examples and references — village, city, joint family,
  generational shifts, festivals, language politics.
- Original prose; no quoting / paraphrasing source text.
- DO NOT include "## Quick reference", "## ही techniques वापरा",
  "## हे टाळा", or numbered technique lists. Those are for howto only.

What works:
- One argument per chapter. State it plainly somewhere in the first third.
- Build the argument with Marathi-context examples — observed life, not
  abstractions.
- A pull-quote (a single bolded line on its own paragraph) is fine if it
  carries the chapter's central claim.
- A closing thought paragraph that lands the reflection is fine.
- Avoid signposting language ("In this chapter we will see…"). Just argue.
-->

<Opening — a concrete observation, scene, or question. Not a thesis
sentence. Earn the reader's attention with something specific.>

<Develop the observation into the chapter's argument over the next few
paragraphs. Use real Marathi-context examples to test the claim. Acknowledge
the obvious counter-argument — essays earn trust by not pretending it
doesn't exist.>

**<Optional pull-quote: one bolded line, on its own paragraph, carrying
the chapter's central claim.>**

<Continue. Push the argument one step further — the non-obvious implication,
the second-order effect, the part that the reader hadn't already thought of.
This is the chapter's reason to exist; if it isn't here, the chapter
collapses into received wisdom.>

<Closing paragraph. Land the reflection on something the reader will carry
with them. Not a checklist, not a moral — a thought.>
